title: The account and the network

story: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, is about to start building RH-1234 on a fresh sandbox VM. Since the image was baked last night, someone merged a pull request that adds a package to the frontend, so the lockfile changed and the VM must run npm ci before any test can pass. The VM sits in a network with no road to the internet, on purpose: if an injected prompt tells Nova to upload our code somewhere, the packets have nowhere to go.

But npm has the same problem. It asks for registry.npmjs.org, the lookup fails, and the install stops with EAI_AGAIN. The same thing will happen tomorrow when FCP Lab, the full product running on the VM with fake data, needs a newer postgres image from Docker Hub. A sandbox that cannot install anything cannot build anything.
hook.question: How does a machine with no road to the internet still install packages and pull images, without opening a road for anything else?

p: The sandbox lives in a box that is built once, in a fixed order. First an AWS account of its own, called ai-agents, so a fooled agent finds no product servers and no customer data next to it. The account carries service control policies, rules set from outside the account that even its administrators cannot change: only one region, and no NAT gateway, no VPC peering and no Transit Gateway, the three ways a private network could get a road out. Then the network inside it: a VPC, AWS's private network, on 10.60.0.0/16, with three private subnets whose only route is local, endpoints to the few AWS services a VM needs, a DNS firewall and a private DNS zone for our own service names. The networks lesson built that VPC on a practice AWS, and the egress lesson put one proxy with a short allow-list in front of it.
So the walls are there. What the box still needs is a way to receive the public packages and images that every build depends on. That is the one idea of this lesson: mirrors.

deeper.h: Go deeper: building the box, step by step
p: A new account arrives empty, and our infrastructure code cannot log in to it yet, because Terragrunt (the tool that runs our OpenTofu code folder by folder) works by assuming a role called TerraformDeploymentRole, and that role does not exist. So the account is created by hand in Control Tower, the AWS tool for an organization of many accounts, the policies are attached there, and the one role is created by hand with the same trust policy as our other accounts. After that, everything is code: an account folder copied from an existing account, a role that only the infrastructure repo's ai-agents environment can use from CI, then the VPC module and its units.

Two of those units matter later. The runs bucket, s3://rhino-ai-agents-runs, keeps every run's transcript and notes for 30 days, encrypted with its own key. And the DNS firewall answers "no such name" for every lookup except the names on its list, which closes the last quiet way out: data hidden inside a DNS lookup. Every plan is run by a person over VPN and pasted into the pull request, and a person applies it.

read.h: A mirror is a registry that fetches for you
p: A mirror, in this sense, is a package registry that we run, which has no packages of its own. Our Nexus server (Nexus is a common tool for hosting package registries) gets a new npm proxy repository whose upstream is registry.npmjs.org. When the sandbox asks it for left-pad 1.3.0 for the first time, Nexus fetches it from npm, stores a copy, and answers. The second sandbox that asks gets the stored copy. The VM only ever talks to Nexus, and Nexus is the one name on the egress proxy's allow-list.

For npm, pointing at the mirror is one line of configuration, and the lockfile then records the mirror's address for every package. The pull-through cache for Docker images works the same way, and a panel below explains it.

code.text:
registry=https://nexus.rhinohealth.com/repository/npmjs/
# HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.ai-agents.rhinohealth.com:3128 is set for every process,
# so this request goes through the egress proxy, which allows nexus.rhinohealth.com and nothing else.

notes.text: npmjs is the name of the npm proxy repository in Nexus. Every npm ci and npm install asks it instead of registry.npmjs.org.

read.see:
$ npm view left-pad version
npm error request to https://registry.npmjs.org/left-pad failed, reason: getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN registry.npmjs.org
$ npm view left-pad version --registry http://mirror:4873
1.3.0

read.h: Why a mirror is not a road out
p: It is fair to ask whether a mirror is just a hole in the wall with a nicer name. The difference is what the sandbox can do through it. Through a mirror the sandbox can ask for a public package by its name and get it back. It cannot choose where the mirror connects, because the upstream is fixed in the mirror's settings, and it cannot store anything, because a proxy repository does not accept uploads and the sandbox has no Nexus credentials to try.

Compare the obvious shortcut: putting registry.npmjs.org itself on the proxy's allow-list. That would work for installs, but npm also accepts uploads. A fooled agent holding a token that an attacker pasted into a ticket could run npm publish and put our code on the public registry, in a package only the attacker knows the name of. Every name on the allow-list is a place a fooled agent can send data. A mirror keeps the list at one name, and that name only reads.
read.see:
$ npm publish --registry http://mirror:4873
npm error code ENEEDAUTH
npm error need auth This command requires you to be logged in to http://mirror:4873/

deeper.h: Go deeper: images, and the mirrors we do not need
p: Docker images get the same treatment from ECR, AWS's container registry. A pull-through cache rule in the ai-agents account says, for example, that any image under the prefix docker-hub/ comes from Docker Hub: the first pull of docker-hub/library/postgres:17 makes ECR fetch it, with our Docker Hub login stored in AWS Secrets Manager, and later pulls come from ECR. The VM reaches ECR through its interface endpoints, so no internet is involved. FCP Lab has to ask for its third-party images with that prefix, which is why the lab needs a registry-prefix setting.

Our own images, the rhino-* images of the product, already live in ECR in our internal account, so the sandbox account only needs permission to pull them. Python packages need nothing new: Nexus already has a PyPI proxy, used by CI today. And the sandbox gets no mirror for GitHub at all: git goes through the broker, the service that holds our GitHub key, which checks every push.

lab.title: Install a package with no road out
needs: About 150 MB for the verdaccio/verdaccio:6 image, a small npm registry that stands in for our Nexus
The node:24-bookworm-slim image (about 350 MB), which plays the sandbox VM
Internet on your laptop, so the mirror can reach registry.npmjs.org
lab.goal: Show that a sandbox with no route out cannot install a package, give it one mirror that fetches from npm for it, and prove that the mirror only reads.

guess.q: A container on a Docker network created with --internal runs npm view left-pad version. What happens?

options.text: It prints the version, because Docker always forwards DNS to your laptop.
options.why: An internal network has no road out, and that includes the lookup for registry.npmjs.org.

options.text: It fails, because npm cannot even look up registry.npmjs.org.
options.why: No route out means no answer for public names either. npm reports EAI_AGAIN, a failed lookup.

options.text: It waits forever, because npm retries without limit.
options.why: npm gives up after a few tries and prints the error.

follow.say: Create the sandbox network with no road out, and see npm fail from inside it.
follow.do:
docker network create --internal g3-2-sandbox
docker run --rm --network g3-2-sandbox node:24-bookworm-slim npm view left-pad version --fetch-retries=0
follow.see:
npm error errno EAI_AGAIN
npm error request to https://registry.npmjs.org/left-pad failed, reason: getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN registry.npmjs.org

follow.say: Start the mirror on Docker's normal network, so it can reach npm, and then also connect it to the sandbox network under the name mirror. It is the only machine on both.
follow.do:
docker run -d --name mirror -p 4873:4873 verdaccio/verdaccio:6
docker network connect --alias mirror g3-2-sandbox mirror

follow.say: Ask the same question from the sandbox, this time to the mirror.
follow.do: docker run --rm --network g3-2-sandbox node:24-bookworm-slim npm view left-pad version --registry http://mirror:4873

follow.say: Install for real and read the lockfile, because the lockfile records where every package came from.
follow.do: docker run --rm --network g3-2-sandbox node:24-bookworm-slim sh -c 'cd /tmp && npm init -y >/dev/null && npm install left-pad@1.3.0 --registry http://mirror:4873 && grep resolved package-lock.json'

follow.say: Look inside the mirror: it kept a copy, so the next sandbox gets it without asking npm.
Now play the fooled agent and try to send something out through the mirror.
follow.do: docker run --rm --network g3-2-sandbox node:24-bookworm-slim sh -c 'mkdir /tmp/p && cd /tmp/p && npm init -y >/dev/null && npm publish --registry http://mirror:4873'
follow.see:
npm error code ENEEDAUTH
npm error need auth This command requires you to be logged in to http://mirror:4873/

lab.build: Make the sandbox use the mirror without a --registry flag on every command, the way the VM's .npmrc does. Write a one-line .npmrc on your laptop, mount it into the sandbox container as /root/.npmrc (docker run -v "$PWD/.npmrc:/root/.npmrc:ro" ...), and install a second package, for example ms@2.1.3, with a plain npm install. Then prove it really came through the mirror: check the resolved line in the lockfile and the mirror's storage folder.
checks: From g3-2-sandbox, npm view against registry.npmjs.org fails with EAI_AGAIN.
The same question with --registry http://mirror:4873 prints 1.3.0.
The lockfile's resolved line starts with http://mirror:4873/.
docker exec mirror ls /verdaccio/storage/data lists every package you installed.
npm publish to the mirror fails with ENEEDAUTH.
You cleaned up: docker rm -f mirror && docker network rm g3-2-sandbox.

solution.file: your terminal, in an empty folder
solution.text:
echo 'registry=http://mirror:4873/' > .npmrc
docker run --rm --network g3-2-sandbox -v "$PWD/.npmrc:/root/.npmrc:ro" node:24-bookworm-slim \
  sh -c 'cd /tmp && npm init -y >/dev/null && npm install ms@2.1.3 && grep resolved package-lock.json'
#       "resolved": "http://mirror:4873/ms/-/ms-2.1.3.tgz",
docker exec mirror ls /verdaccio/storage/data
# left-pad
# ms

lab.fix: A teammate was tired of slow first installs and gave the sandbox a road out "just for npm": docker network connect bridge <the sandbox container>. Recreate it with a long-running sandbox (docker run -d --name vm --network g3-2-sandbox node:24-bookworm-slim sleep 600, then docker network connect bridge vm). From docker exec vm, show that npm now reaches registry.npmjs.org directly, and that so does curl to any other site you like, which is the real damage. Disconnect the bridge network again and prove npm only works through the mirror.
explain: What exactly does the sandbox do when it installs a package that the mirror has never seen?
Why is a mirror safer than putting registry.npmjs.org on the egress proxy's allow-list?
How do Docker images reach the sandbox when FCP Lab needs a new postgres image?
lab.done: The sandbox installs packages only through the mirror, the mirror keeps a copy of each, and a publish through it is refused.

check.q: The sandbox runs npm ci against the Nexus mirror, and one package in the lockfile has never been requested before. What happens?

options.text: The install fails, because the mirror has no copy yet
options.why: A proxy repository is made for exactly this case: a missing package is fetched from its upstream on the first request.

options.text: The mirror tells npm to fetch that package from registry.npmjs.org itself
options.why: The sandbox has no route to npm, so that could not work. The mirror fetches on the sandbox's behalf.

options.text: The mirror fetches it from npm, keeps a copy and returns it; the sandbox only ever talks to the mirror
options.why: That is a pull-through mirror: first request fetches and stores, later requests are served from the copy.

check.q: A teammate suggests putting registry.npmjs.org on the egress proxy's allow-list instead of running a mirror. What is the risk?

options.text: npm also accepts uploads, so a fooled agent with a pasted token could publish our code to the public registry
options.why: Every allowed name is a place data can go. The mirror only reads, and the sandbox has no credentials for it.

options.text: Installs become slower, because npm is far away
options.why: Speed is a small benefit of the mirror's copies. The reason is that the sandbox could send data out.

options.text: The allow-list cannot hold domain names
options.why: It holds names, for example nexus.rhinohealth.com. The question is which names are safe to hold.

check.q: An injected prompt tells Nova to run npm publish against the mirror, to get our code out. What happens?

options.text: It works, because the mirror is on the allow-list
options.why: Reaching the mirror is allowed, but the mirror decides what it accepts, and a proxy repository does not accept uploads.

options.text: It is refused: the mirror needs a login for uploads, and the sandbox has no credentials for it
options.why: The sandbox can ask for public packages by name, nothing more. That is what makes the one allowed name safe.

options.text: The mirror forwards the upload to registry.npmjs.org
options.why: A proxy repository fetches from its upstream; it never sends uploads to it.

p: The ai-agents account is created in Control Tower with SCPs for us-east-1 only, no leaving the organization, and no VPC peering, Transit Gateway attachments or NAT gateways for anyone but TerraformDeploymentRole, which is bootstrapped by hand. terraform/accounts/ai-agents/ is copied from the solutions account, with a GitHub Actions role that trusts only the infrastructure repo's ai-agents environment. modules/aws-vpc-private is a copy of modules/aws-vpc with no public subnets, internet gateway or NAT, flow logs always on, an S3 gateway endpoint limited to our buckets and interface endpoints with private DNS.

The VPC unit uses 10.60.0.0/16 (confirm it is free with DevOps), allows the runs bucket and ECR's layer bucket on the S3 endpoint, and adds endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages, ec2messages, ecr.api, ecr.dkr, logs and autoscaling. Next to it: the runs bucket rhino-ai-agents-runs (own KMS key, versioning, 30-day expiry), the Route 53 DNS firewall and the private zone ai-agents.rhinohealth.com. The mirrors: an npm proxy repository npmjs in modules/nexus-oss next to the PyPI one, ECR pull-through cache rules for Docker Hub and public ECR, and pull access to inf ECR for the ai-agents account.

tickets.why: The account, its SCPs, the hand-made deploy role and the Terragrunt tree.
The VPC unit, the DNS firewall, the private zone and the runs bucket.
The mirrors: the Nexus npm proxy, the ECR pull-through cache and access to our own images.

words.plain: A package registry we run that fetches public packages for machines with no road out, and keeps a copy.
A repository in Nexus with no packages of its own: it fetches from one fixed upstream and does not accept uploads.
The same idea for container images: ECR fetches an image from Docker Hub on the first pull and serves its copy after that.
The real registry a mirror fetches from, such as registry.npmjs.org. It is fixed in the mirror's settings.
A rule set from outside an AWS account that limits everyone in it, administrators included.

review.q: Draw the path of one npm ci request from the sandbox VM to registry.npmjs.org, naming each machine.
review.a: npm on the VM, through HTTPS_PROXY to the Squid egress proxy, which allows nexus.rhinohealth.com; Nexus serves its copy or fetches from registry.npmjs.org. The VM never talks to npm.

review.q: FCP Lab on the VM needs postgres:17 from Docker Hub. How does it get it, and what must FCP Lab support for that?
review.a: Through an ECR pull-through cache rule: it pulls docker-hub/library/postgres:17 from ECR over the VM's endpoints, and ECR fetches from Docker Hub the first time. FCP Lab must accept a registry prefix for third-party images.

remember: Seal the box, then let packages in through mirrors we run: one name on the list, which fetches public packages for the sandbox and accepts nothing from it.
